Newly hatched neonates of Daphnia schoedleri exhibit a total length at birth of 0.068 cm [Lb = 0.068 cm], a diminutive size that reflects the constrained space within the brood chamber of the maternal exoskeleton. This initial body dimension is typical for daphniids that undergo a rapid, univoltine growth trajectory early in the season. At a standard laboratory temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the time elapsed from oviposition to the onset of exogenous filter feeding, termed the age at birth, is approximately 2.5 days [ab = approximately 2.5 days]. This brief embryonic period is energetically fueled by the yolk reserves of the subitaneous egg, allowing the first-instar juvenile to commence phytoplankton grazing almost immediately upon release. Such a compressed developmental schedule is an adaptation to ephemeral pond environments, where rapid generation turnover maximizes population growth before habitat desiccation or predation pressure escalates. The transition from yolk dependence to active feeding marks a critical nutritional threshold, after which somatic growth becomes entirely dependent on the individual's filtration efficiency and the prevailing seston concentration. This species thus exhibits a life history finely tuned to exploit transient aquatic habitats.

As juveniles progress through successive instars, they undergo a predictable pattern of linear growth punctuated by ecdysis. Under the same thermal regime of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the time since birth at which individuals first attain morphological and gonadal markers of puberty has been measured at 3.2 days [tp = 3.2 days]. Correspondingly, the total length recorded at this developmental milestone is 0.15 cm [Lp = 0.15 cm], a length that signifies the onset of reproductive competence. This rapid maturation is among the fastest documented within the genus Daphnia, likely favored in habitats with intense but unpredictable abiotic fluctuations. Attaining puberty in just over three days permits the first brood of parthenogenetic eggs to be deposited into the brood chamber with minimal delay, thereby accelerating intrinsic population growth. The total length at puberty is about two-thirds of the length at birth, underscoring how profoundly somatic growth transforms the body plan within the first 72 hours of post-embryonic life.

Following puberty, individuals continue to add body mass and linear dimension through successive molts until they asymptotically approach their ultimate total length. For this population of Daphnia schoedleri maintained under optimal food conditions at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the adult carapace length plateaus at approximately 0.35 cm [Li = approximately 0.35 cm], a moderate size relative to other daphniids but sufficient to accommodate multiple developing embryos. The corresponding ultimate dry weight for such adults has been estimated at 508.0 micrograms , a value derived from allometric scaling relationships validated in the closely related model species Daphnia magna. This mass reflects the accumulation of both structural tissues and transient lipid stores that sustain repeated reproductive episodes. Gravid females at this size exhibit a noticeably distended brood chamber, visible even under low magnification, which can house a clutch of several parthenogenetic eggs depending on nutritional history and maternal age. The asymptotic body size sets an upper bound on the individual's filtration capacity and thus on its potential for resource acquisition.

This duration encompasses multiple reproductive cycles, during which senescent declines in clutch size and neonate viability become apparent in the terminal weeks of life. The post-reproductive period is characterized by a gradual loss of swimming vigor and a decreased ability to evade tactile predators such as Chaoborus larvae. Field surveys indicate that very few individuals in natural populations attain this theoretical maximum, as mortality from fish predation, starvation, and parasitism truncates survival far earlier. Nonetheless, the laboratory-measured lifespan provides a valuable benchmark for comparing intrinsic senescence rates among congeneric species, revealing that D. schoedleri possesses a moderately paced life history relative to smaller-bodied daphniids which often complete their entire life cycle in under sixty days.
